extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor-union representatives, labor/employment counsel, human-resources professionals, and other stakeholders affected by NLRB joint-employer rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive and explanatory guidance accompanying the NLRB's final rule on when an entity is a 'joint employer' under the NLRA, including which terms and conditions of employment are 'essential' and what forms/quantum of control are probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive list of essential terms and conditions of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes an exhaustive list of 'essential terms and conditions of employment' that the Board will treat as material to the existence of a common-law employment relationship for joint-employer purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board adopted an exhaustive list to offer clearer guidance and more predictable standards; because the list is exhaustive, the Board declined to add other terms but recognizes bargaining over certain subjects (e.g., workplace surveillance) may be important once joint-employer status is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling and hours of work are essential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Scheduling, together with hours of work, is included as an essential term or condition of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Restatement (Second) of Agency and Board precedent treating scheduling as probative of joint-employer status; scheduling practices are often intertwined with hours of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace health and safety as an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: Control over workplace health and safety is an essential term or condition of employment indicative of a common-law employment relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common-law support links employer control over 'the physical conduct' of employees to employment relationships; acknowledging existing regulatory schemes (OSHA etc.), mere incorporation of regulatory requirements into contracts without reserving authority to control or exercising control is not indicative of joint-employer status. The COVID-19 pandemic reinforces its importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work rules and directions governing manner, means, or methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing or exercising control over work rules or directions governing the manner, means, or methods of work performance is an essential term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Restatement sections and commenters' views that such control illuminates the extent of control over work details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of authority to control suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing the authority to control one or more essential terms or conditions of employment is sufficient to establish status as a joint employer, regardless of whether that control is exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule treats reserved authority as probative; the inquiry follows common-law agency principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control and control through intermediaries are sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercising the power to control indirectly or through an intermediary person or entity can be sufficient to establish joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board retained general common-law language so the rule can be applied to diverse mechanisms (e.g., franchisors, staffing, temporary employment), and follows the D.C. Circuit that the common law does not permit intermediaries to be used to avoid a master-servant relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 'substantial direct and immediate control' limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board rejected a rule-wide limitation that only 'substantial direct and immediate control' gives rise to joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Board must apply common-law agency principles, it will not incorporate an additional restriction requiring direct and immediate exercise of control; courts and precedents guide application to facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum/type of control resolved case-by-case under common-law agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of a particular quantum or type of indirect or reserved control to establish joint-employer status will be assessed under common-law agency principles on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board declined to specify in the rule every form or quantum of control (e.g., surveillance, budgetary nonwage controls) so future application can consider context and avoid over- or under-inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control that merely embodies legal/regulatory requirements is not probative
rubrics_metrics.description: If a law or regulation sets a particular term and an entity merely embodies or memorializes that requirement in its contracts without reserving or exercising authority to control the terms or conditions, that does not make the entity an employer of the third-party's employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flow-down clauses required by statute or contract (e.g., Service Contract Act, Davis-Bacon) typically do not create a common-law employment relationship because they are not discretionary or subject to collective bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of public entities from 'employer' definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2(2) of the Act excludes public entities (e.g., United States, wholly owned Government corporations, Federal Reserve Banks, states or political subdivisions) from the statutory definition of 'employer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a public entity possesses or exercises control over essential terms, that exclusion means it is not a joint employer for purposes of the Act; the Board will apply precedent (e.g., Management Training Corp.) when assessing government contractors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over matters immaterial to common-law employment is irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of control over matters immaterial to the existence of an employment relationship under common-law agency principles, or control over matters that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions of employment, is not relevant to determining joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board follows the D.C. Circuit's approach that 'routine components of a company-to-company contract' are generally not material; examples provided in the rulemaking illustrate typical non-probative components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of contractual provisions typically not probative
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-exhaustive collection of company-to-company contract provisions that often resemble routine business terms and are typically not probative of a common-law employment relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page enumerates many illustrations (not adopted as an exclusive list) including: objectives/basic ground rules/expectations; advance descriptions of tasks; instructions about what/where/when to perform work; minimum staffing requirements; quality/productivity/timing/safety terms; delivery-window requirements; brand/design/logo/image/brand standards maintenance; uniform requirements; general visitor rules; general price terms; authority to cancel a contract (including at will); background checks/drug tests/licensure requirements; authority to bar or reject particular individuals; property/premises/equipment control terms (including training and safety requirements); confidentiality/IP protections; construction project schedules/site-specific safety programs; parties' obligations under law/regulation; hospital superintendence of contract employees; DEIA/CSR/ESG goals; cost-plus arrangements; minimum compensation set by public contracting rules (e.g., Davis-Bacon). The Board nonetheless declined to categorically codify all these as immaterial and will evaluate context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring for quality assurance/auditing is generally not probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Monitoring a third party's performance for quality assurance or auditing for compliance with contractual obligations will generally not be viewed as probative of joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged clarification; the Board declined to adopt a categorical rule and will consider such practices in context under common-law principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchisor brand-protection controls often immaterial but not categorically exempt
rubrics_metrics.description: Many steps franchisors take to protect brands (logos, store design/decor, product uniformity) typically have no connection to essential terms and so will not indicate a common-law employment relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will not categorically state all brand-protection controls are immaterial, but the exhaustive list of essential terms aims to give franchisors clearer guidance about what controls are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments for payroll services generally not sufficient to show wage control
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a payment as part of a contract to provide payroll services is not, by itself, sufficient to demonstrate control over wages adequate to support a joint-employer finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters raised this example; the Board did not modify the rule text to address every such scenario and will assess context and reserved/exercised authority in application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction-industry practices do not automatically establish joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared or oversight responsibilities inherent in construction jobsites (e.g., general contractor overall responsibility) are not alone probative of a common-law employment relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board follows Supreme Court precedent (Denver Building) that a general contractor is not the employer of a subcontractor's employees solely because of overall jobsite oversight; there must be evidence of control over essential terms for joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining obligation of a joint employer
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an entity is found to be a joint employer because it shares or codetermines matters governing one or more employees' essential terms and conditions, it is obligated to bargain over any mandatory subjects of bargaining that it possesses or exercises the authority to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule clarifies that the obligation is limited to mandatory subjects the joint employer controls; the Board will adhere to precedent (e.g., First National Maintenance) holding that core entrepreneurial decisions changing scope/direction of enterprise are not mandatory subjects of bargaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limits when other entities control terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a common-law employer lacks control over certain terms because those terms are controlled by an exempt or third-party entity, the common-law employer is not required to bargain about those terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, a joint employer will be required to bargain only over subjects it possesses or exercises authority to control; contractually imposed basic expectations or ground rules that do not reserve authority or exercise control over the manner/methods of performance do not suffice to make an entity an employer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to independent-contractor precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent-contractor cases may be instructive to the joint-employer inquiry to the extent they illuminate the nature and extent of control necessary to establish a common-law employment relationship, but the standards are distinct and must be carefully distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters criticized reliance on independent-contractor precedent; Board recognizes differences but will use such precedent as relevant on questions of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for asserting joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: The party asserting joint-employer status bears the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that a putative joint employer satisfies the rule's requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No commenters urged reallocating this burden; the Board retained proposed paragraph (g) allocating the burden to the asserting party.
